title: Uniform constant-factor information bound for best-arm identification
formal:
Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) and a family of sequential sampling procedures \((A_{K,\delta})_{K\ge2,\ 0<\delta<1/4}\) such that, for every vector \(\mu\in\mathbb R^K\) with a unique largest coordinate, the procedure identifies its largest-mean arm with probability at least \(1-\delta\) and its stopping time satisfies
\[
\mathbb E_\mu[\tau]\le C\,T^*(\mu)\log(1/\delta)?
\]
The arms are independent Gaussian distributions \(N(\mu_i,1)\), their means are unknown, and the procedures receive neither a lower bound on the positive gaps nor any other information about \(\mu\). The characteristic time \(T^*\) is defined below. The answer to this selected uniform finite-time target is negative, already for two arms.
why: A sampling allocation tailored to known gaps can be much cheaper than discovering how small the gaps are. The negative result identifies why an asymptotically sharp information bound cannot be used unchanged as a uniform finite-time guarantee.
status_note: Resolved negatively for the explicitly selected uniform constant-factor target by the two-arm unknown-gap iterated-logarithm lower bound, as stated in Jamieson et al. (COLT 2014) from Farrell (1964). The broader 2020 questions about finite-time instance dependence and simple regret are not declared resolved by this archive. Selection is an announced editorial default after an unanswered optional question. category_assignment.reason: Finite-time best-arm identification and simple regret concern sequential exploration under bandit feedback.

importance.reason: The distinction between an information lower bound and the cost of adapting to unknown gaps is central to experimental design. This selected negative target provides a precise limit on uniform finite-time optimality, while broader instance-optimal characterization remains a separate question.

sentences: The task samples independent Gaussian arms to identify the one with largest unknown mean.
It asks whether a single instance-independent procedure can match the information lower bound within one universal constant at every confidence level and instance.
Already two arms force an extra iterated-logarithm cost along some sequences of shrinking gaps.
Thus the selected uniform finite-time target has a known negative answer.
This archival does not settle every broader question about instance-optimal sampling or simple regret.

definitions:
For \(K\ge2\), set \([K]=\{1,\ldots,K\}\) and let \(i^*(\mu)\) be the unique maximizer of \(\mu_i\). For each arm \(i\), there is an infinite sequence of independent samples with Gaussian mean \(\mu_i\) and variance one, and these sequences are mutually independent. Pulling arm \(i\) reveals its next unused sample as an exact real number. The family of possible instances contains every real mean vector with a unique best arm; equality of two nonmaximal means is allowed.

A procedure initially knows only \(K,\delta\) and the variance-one Gaussian model. Using private independent randomness and all past arm indices and observations, it selects the next arm or stops and recommends one index \(\widehat i\in[K]\). Choices, stopping rules and recommendations must be measurable with respect to the observations already obtained and the procedure's randomness. No computation or memory limit is imposed. For every allowed instance the procedure must stop almost surely and satisfy \(\Pr_\mu(\widehat i\ne i^*(\mu))\le\delta\). Its cost \(\tau\) is the total number of samples from all arms. Correctness is required on every allowed instance for the same procedure at the given \(K,\delta\); it cannot be selected after the unknown mean vector is revealed.

Let \(\Delta_K=\{w\in[0,1]^K:\sum_iw_i=1\}\) and let \(\operatorname{Alt}(\mu)\) be the set of vectors \(\lambda\in\mathbb R^K\) with a unique largest coordinate whose maximizing index differs from \(i^*(\mu)\). Using natural logarithms, define
\[
T^*(\mu)=\left[\sup_{w\in\Delta_K}\inf_{\lambda\in\operatorname{Alt}(\mu)}
\frac12\sum_{i=1}^K w_i(\mu_i-\lambda_i)^2\right]^{-1}.
\]
The denominator is positive and finite for every allowed vector. The factor \((\mu_i-\lambda_i)^2/2\) is the relative entropy between the corresponding variance-one Gaussian laws. This benchmark assumes an allocation optimized for the true instance, although the sampling procedure is not given that instance. The supremum and infimum are part of the definition, not computational resources available to the learner.

The assertion chooses one finite \(C\) for all arm counts, error levels and mean vectors. A different procedure is permitted for each known pair \((K,\delta)\). In particular, the target is stronger than a bound only as \(\delta\to0\) with \(\mu\) fixed, stronger than a bound with an instance-dependent additive term, and different from optimizing a separate everywhere-correct procedure for each individual instance. No promise separates the best two means by a known amount.

For two arms of means \(0,\Delta\), with \(\Delta\ne0\), direct optimization in this definition gives \(T^*=8/\Delta^2\). With any fixed \(\delta<1/4\), the proposed inequality would therefore bound the expected sample count by a constant times \(\Delta^{-2}\), uniformly as \(\Delta\) approaches zero from either side. The established iterated-logarithm obstruction instead gives a positive limsup after dividing the sample count by \(\Delta^{-2}\log\log(\Delta^{-2})\). This is an obstruction along some arbitrarily small gaps, not a claim of that extra cost at every fixed gap.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed existence assertion. For a refutation it suffices to fix an allowed error level and show that no two-arm procedure can satisfy the uniform characteristic-time bound. The cited classical obstruction supports archival; no completed Lean verification of it is asserted.

context_blocks.text: The textbook proves a characteristic-time lower bound and discusses matching it asymptotically as the error probability vanishes at a fixed instance. Its broader research discussion does not equate that limit with a uniform finite-time theorem.

The 2014 paper states the two-arm iterated-logarithm lower bound, deriving it from Farrell’s 1964 sequential-testing result. A positive limsup as the unknown gap tends to zero contradicts the selected uniform bound.

A September 2026 preprint claims a broader gap-entropy characterization. Its stated uniform upper bound explicitly retains an additive iterated-logarithm term. The present archival rests on the established two-arm obstruction, not on verification of that new preprint’s full proofs.
